alalal-e80886-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 10: by what form faith is formed.

alalal-e80886-d1e111.summary: States the second question of the series: by what form is faith formed.

alalal-e80886-d1e118.summary: First argument for grace: faith needs only to tend toward what it believes in a pleasing way, which grace provides.

alalal-e80886-d1e130.summary: Second argument for grace: unformed faith believes all that formed faith does but lacks merit, and grace is what makes acts meritorious.

alalal-e80886-d1e141.summary: Argument for charity: Lombard's text seems to say charity forms faith.

alalal-e80886-d1e150.summary: Further: charity is the mother of all virtues, so of faith too.

alalal-e80886-d1e159.summary: Further: forming belongs to what never becomes unformed, which is charity.

alalal-e80886-d1e168.summary: Sed contra: form gives species and ratio, so if charity informed faith, faith would be charity.

alalal-e80886-d1e181.summary: Second sed contra: what is divided against another species under the same genus is not its form; charity and faith are co-divided under theological virtue.

alalal-e80886-d1e200.summary: Similarly, grace as grace does not inform: what is found with the same ratio in many species is not the form of any one, since things are distinguished by their forms; grace makes pleasing equally in all virtues.

alalal-e80886-d1e235.summary: Solution: faith is formed by its own proper form, as every virtue is: a light informing the affective intellect with respect to tending toward the end, formal relative to the habit of assenting to God. In act, faith assents to first truth for its own sake and above all; adding tending into what it assents to adds nothing material but the perfection of attaining the end, which is the principal form in moral matters and virtues. So in the habit, a further light is added that joins the believer's intellect to the truth it believes.
claims: Faith is formed by its own proper form, a light that orders the affective intellect toward its end.
The form of faith adds the perfection of tending into first truth, not any new material content.

alalal-e80886-d1e281.summary: Reply to the first argument: being pleasing in itself is not enough; there must be something specifying faith by which it tends to first truth as first truth.

alalal-e80886-d1e294.summary: Reply to the second: it is not true that faith needs only merit; there must be something specifying the habit so that it elicits the meritorious acts proper to this virtue.

alalal-e80886-d1e310.summary: Reply on charity: charity is not a form giving being but one giving well-being, as will appear later.
claims: Charity gives faith well-being, not being.

alalal-e80886-d1e321.summary: Reply on 'mother': being mother does not make charity the form giving being; it is called mother because the virtues are formed in its womb in a certain qualified sense of being.

alalal-e80886-d1e340.summary: Reply to the third: charity never becomes unformed, but this gives it a role in well-being, not being, since things differing in species must have different forms.

alalal-e80886.summary: Article 10 asks what form forms faith: grace, which makes acts pleasing and meritorious, or charity, the mother of the virtues that never becomes unformed. Against both, a form gives species, so charity as a form would make faith charity, and grace, the same in all virtues, cannot specify any one of them. Albert holds that faith is formed by its own proper form. This is a light informing the affective intellect toward the end, which adds to the act of assenting to first truth the perfection of tending into it and being joined to it. Grace alone does not specify, and charity gives faith well-being rather than being; it is called mother because the virtues are formed within it in a qualified sense.
claims: Faith is formed by its own proper form, a light ordering the affective intellect toward its end.
Neither grace nor charity is the form that gives faith its being.
Charity gives faith well-being, not specific being.
